Security follow-up scheduled.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-28
Time: 14:00 PT / 21:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Sophie (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Maya (Ridgewell Head of ML), Carlos (Eng Manager), Liam (Security)

[00:00] Sophie: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick roll call, can you hear me?
[00:07] Maya: yes i can, sorry had a quick calendar conflict but i'm here now
[00:12] Carlos: here
[00:13] Liam: here
[00:15] Daniel: good morning/afternoon folks, daniel from redwood

[02:10] Sophie: Alright quick agenda — recap last week's tuning, quality evals on the new prompt set, regression checks (esp lab values and clinical entities), and next steps. Maya you had some new scoring feedback?
[02:22] Maya: yeah, so we ran the latest prompt set you sent Friday, scored on 1-5 for clinical correctness and for hallucination risk. overall precision improved from 0.81 to 0.86 but recall dropped a bit on lab values — so we're seeing misses on things like eGFR ranges and sodium levels when phrased unconventionally.

[04:05] Daniel: interesting, do you have examples? is it the prompt wording or the system default temperature?
[04:12] Maya: both maybe, here's one — question was 'what's typical egfr for a 65 year old with crcl 45' and model returned a generic range, missed the nuance. sometimes it substitutes creatinine clearance (crcl) and we see confusion, probably tokenization or aliasing.

[06:00] Carlos: also saw more guardrail hits on PHI masking, we're getting false positives where normal medication names are flagged as sensitive and that hurts throughput for our downstream annotator.

[06:28] Sophie: that's helpful. on the guardrails we added a heuristic last week to err on the side of caution, which will increase false positives — we can relax threshold or add allowlist for common meds. Daniel — quick note: we shipped a small fix to the regex-based detector, but we should probably move to a list-based allowlist for Ridgewell.
[06:45] Daniel: yep, we can do that. i'll add a per-customer allowlist into the pipeline, and we can make it editable in the console so your data team can tune without us.

[09:15] Maya: about scoring rubric — a couple of things: the 'partial credit' rules aren't consistent. for entity extraction you give 0.5 for partial match but sometimes it counts as zero because of punctuation mismatches. the scoring script also mis-parses tokens that look like 'Na+' as 'Na' and that changes match.
[09:42] Daniel: okay that sounds like a tokenizer mismatch between the scoring harness and the model output. i'll patch the scorer to normalize chemical notations and strip punctuation before matching.

[12:00] Sophie: Thanks. on the perf side, we saw per-request latency at 320ms average in hosted mode for your typical 256-token prompts, does that align with what you saw?
[12:12] Carlos: we observed averages closer to 350ms with spikes to 900ms during peak test windows. some of that is our network but i suspect batching behavior.

[13:30] Daniel: two notes — our hosted deployment uses dynamic batching and prefix cache; during peak concurrency batching increases throughput but some requests can hit cold start cost if you have high variance. Dedicated will give you pinned capacity which flattens latency, but cost is higher. i'll run a dedicated vs hosted comparison tuned to your concurrency profile.

[15:05] Maya: would be great to see the tradeoffs especially since our SLA needs 99th percentile under 700ms.

[16:20] Liam: quick sec on security — we need clarification on KMS integration and audit log retention for the pilot. last call mentioned optional customer-managed KMS in private, what about dedicated?
[16:35] Sophie: Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS via the private controls, hosted we offer server-side encryption and we can do bring-your-own-key for Dedicated and Private. for hosted we can also provide detailed audit logs for request/response metadata but not full plaintext unless we set up a private endpoint.
[16:56] Liam: ok need to check legal on storing request payloads; also what's retention on logs?
[17:03] Daniel: default retention is 90 days, we can extend as an add-on. i'll share the SOC2 docs and the audit log SLA notes after this call.

[19:00] Carlos: back to quality — i noticed one regression where the model started hallucinating vendor product names when asked about imaging devices. could be from the new prompt example that mentions specific vendors.
[19:18] Maya: yes we found that too — when the prompt contains sample EHR notes that include vendor terms, the model sometimes generalizes and invents specs.

[20:40] Sophie: hmm that suggests the prompt injection is leaking. best practice is to sanitize sample notes or use bracketed placeholders. we'll update the prompt templates.

[22:10] Daniel: another idea — we can run a differential eval between model version A (current) and B (tuned) using your regression suite and return per-case diffs and a 'win/loss' table. i've set up the eval harness to output CSV and a sample-by-sample diff; want that?
[22:26] Maya: yes please, that would help prioritize fixes.

[24:00] Sophie: ok let's talk scoring discrepancies — Maya said the scorer gives partial credit inconsistently. can you run a normalization pass and re-score last week's 2k prompts?
[24:14] Daniel: yes, i'll normalize Na+/Na, strip punctuation, lower-case when appropriate, and re-run the 2k set overnight. i'll upload results to the shared folder with a notes doc.

[26:30] Maya: can you also add a column for 'guardrail false positive' in the eval output so we can filter those out when computing precision/recall?
[26:40] Daniel: yea that makes sense — i'll add a boolean flag per-case and include the original raw model output for traceability.

[28:55] Carlos: one more perf question — how does KV cache hit rate impact latency? we saw 30% hit rate in our test but theory suggests caching should bump to ~60% with prefix grouping.
[29:10] Daniel: Cache hit rate is workload dependent; for user-session style queries you'll get better hits. i can run a synthetic test with your traffic patterns and try different TTLs to estimate benefits.

[31:00] Maya: great. on guardrails: if we relax the PHI detector threshold, we worry about potential compliance hits. what's your recommended middle ground?
[31:12] Sophie: recommended is to maintain conservative detection for hosted prod, but for pilot we can use a relaxed threshold and manual review queue — that reduces false positives while keeping an audit trail. we can also implement per-customer allowlist to avoid known meds being flagged.

[33:40] Liam: for the security follow-up, i'll need explicit notes on what fields are logged, how PII is redacted, and the retention policy. also please confirm data residency options if we move to private deployment.
[33:55] Sophie: noted — i'll include a matrix of logged fields and redaction behavior. private deployment supports region locking and can be packaged on-prem for strict residency.

[36:00] Daniel: next steps recap: i'll re-run scoring normalization and the 2k re-score; i'll add guardrail false positive flag and run the dedicated vs hosted perf/cost sim. Sophie will share prompt set and updated prompt templates with placeholders; Maya will upload failure cases.

[37:20] Maya: timeline looks good. will try to surface top failure cases by next Tuesday.

[38:40] Sophie: Anything else?
[38:45] Carlos: just one ask — can we get an export of raw tokens for a sample of requests for debugging?
[38:53] Daniel: yes we can provide anonymized token traces for debugging, we'll sanitize PHI before sharing.

[40:10] Liam: thanks all — i'll follow up if legal needs more.

[41:00] Sophie: ok thanks everyone. i'll send notes and the prompt set after the call. recap of action items in the doc.

Shared artifacts mentioned: link: https://redwood.app/drive/ridgewell/prompt-sets/latest (Sophie to share), security deck (SOC2 + KMS notes), perf spreadsheet (Daniel)

Meeting end.
